**Ch 019 draft, paragraph beginning "This eccentricity did not mean strength..."**

> "He had his collision with Palmerston; he drove Russell off the field; he overbore Slidell; but he never lifted a finger against Mason, who became his bulwark of defence."

The subject "he" here refers to Mr. Adams. In the source the sentence reads: "He had his collision with Palmerston; he drove Russell off the field; he swept the board before Cockburn; he overbore Slidell; but he never lifted a finger against Mason." In the draft, the preceding sentences are about Mason, not Adams — the draft says "Mason was his greatest diplomatic triumph. He had his collision with Palmerston…" The pronoun "he" has an ambiguous antecedent: is it Mason or Adams? In the source the paragraph makes clear that Adams is the subject throughout, but in the draft the immediately preceding named subject is Mason, and the sentence "Mason was his greatest diplomatic triumph" places Mason as the topic noun. A competent reader could genuinely be confused about whether it is Mason or Adams who "drove Russell off the field."

However, re-reading: "Mr. Adams had his usual luck in enemies… Mason was his greatest diplomatic triumph. He had his collision with Palmerston…" — the "his" in "Mason was his greatest diplomatic triumph" anchors Adams as the possessive subject, and "He had his collision" most naturally continues Adams as subject. A careful reader would likely resolve this to Adams. This is at the boundary, but I think a competent reader would parse it correctly, making it merely less ornate rather than genuinely confusing. I will not flag this.

"That scene in the House of Commons" — the draft's previous paragraph establishes the scene in the House of Commons (the Roebuck debate, June 30, 1863). The definite "that scene" has a clear antecedent. No issue.

**Ch 018 draft: "Russell's reply of September 5 reached the Legation on September 8..."**

A competent reader would be misled into thinking Russell replied on September 5, when the source makes clear that September 5 is Adams's note date and the reply arrived September 8. This is a genuine ambiguity introduced by compression.

This passes the gate test: a reader with no source access would read "Russell's reply of September 5" as a reply dated September 5, but the reply arrived on September 8 — that is contradictory and confusing. The reader cannot resolve which date belongs to which document without the source's clarifying "to this note of."
